div.p: The department solves first, then records. Encoding is a record of work done, not a queue of work to do. That single fact shapes everything here.

Creation can enter any of the three states. The thick green arrow is the normal case: the concern was fixed on the spot, and the ticket is written straight to Closed. A model that forced every ticket to start at Open and be clicked through to Closed would make staff perform a three-step workflow to record a fix they already made — the fastest way to get a system abandoned in favour of the spreadsheet.
Open is rare and real. It means logged but not yet attempted — reported when nobody could act on it yet. It is not a mandatory first stop.

Closed is terminal. There is no reopen. A recurring problem is a new ticket. This is a deliberate departmental rule, and it has a consequence worth stating: a printer that fails four times produces four tickets, not one ticket closed four times. Volume counts will reflect that, and they should — recurrence frequency becomes visible rather than hidden inside one ticket's history.

There is no Voided status. Encoding mistakes are corrected by editing the ticket, and the audit log preserves what changed. Tickets are never deleted: deletion would leave a gap in the number sequence and orphan the row already written to the sheet.

ongoing_at is what makes first-time fix rate measurable. A ticket closed with ongoing_at IS NULL was fixed on the spot; one with a value went Ongoing first. No extra column is needed to tell those apart.
Every transition writes an audit entry and a sync outbox row in the same transaction as the status change. There is no path that changes status without both.
